If the soul within is more real than the outer world, as you, philosopher, pretend, why then is it the outer world that is offered to me as the model of reality?
—Fernando Pessoa, Poèmes Païens: d'Alberto Caeiro et de
Ricardo Reis.

For many years I have endeavored to capture a glimpse of the mysterious origins of creative expression, through exploring the impact that certain creative works have on me, as well as by studying the creative process and its inhibitions in my analysands. In whatever form of expression—writing, painting, sculpture, music, the performing arts, scientific and intellectual creativity, or innovation in the world of politics, business, and industrial invention—there is an enigmatic dimension to creative activity that evades our comprehension.

Freud (1908) himself searched constantly for the secrets of creativity. In his essay "Creative Writers and Day Dreaming," he asks: "From what sources does that strange being [the creative writer] draw his material?" He replies that a creative writer behaves like a child at play in that he creates a world of his own. He states that the child "creates a world of phantasy which he takes very seriously [and] invests with large amounts of emotion." Freud goes on to say, "as people grow up they cease to play [and furthermore the adult] knows that he is expected not to go on playing or phantasying any longer." Later in the same essay he proclaims, "we may lay it down that a happy person never phantasies, only an unsatisfied one." This somewhat critical attitude to fantasy life in adulthood appears throughout Freud's writings, as though fantasies, and even the enjoyment of contemplating creative works, were preoccupations about which he felt guilty.

THIS PAPER ADDRESSES SOME ASPECTS of the question, how psychoanalysis may be therapeutic. It begins with excerpts from a session in which disturbingly vivid dreams were reported by and discussed with the patient. It concludes with a brief consideration of the nature of the remedial effects of psychoanalytic work.

My discussion applies basically to situations where the patient can cooperate in the endeavor. This point seems worth mentioning, to introduce a measure of balance. Many, perhaps most claimed advances in analytic theory stress the role of the analyst in modifying understanding (insight) or technical approach (empathy), even when the advance is characterized as interpersonal, implying emphasis on the presence of and interaction with the other person. The accent falls on the value of the analyst's recognizing affirmative possibilities in phenomena previously seen as obstacles to analysis, such as resistance and countertransference. Part of my emphasis in this discussion is on the role of the patient's aim, participation, and responsibility in the process. This could supplement and also balance the prevalent, often one-sided, emphasis on traumatization and victimhood.

It may be useful to reflect on whether we regard analysis as meant primarily to inflame the sense of hurt and outrage that are often awakened during the work, or as meant to help face and master, where possible, and, where not, to come to terms with, the consequences of injury and personal limitations.

DONALD SPENCE (1988), SUMMARIZING a workshop entitled "How Does Treatment Help?" proposed the following:

Theories … are all comforting to the degree that they suggest that we know something about how and why treatment works. … They comfort even more because they shield us from ignorance and from the knowledge that we have, at bottom, very little real understanding of the therapeutic process; a meager supply of facts; and almost nothing in the way of cumulative findings. (p. 190)

Perhaps this is an overly pessimistic appraisal of the first century of psychoanalytic practice. However, it does speak to our difficulty in making useful generalizations from accumulated clinical experience. Jay Greenberg Ph.D.

Jay Greenberg

Jay Greenberg, Ph.D.
275 Central Park West, 1BB
New York, N.Y. 10024

Jay Greenberg  

WHEN PSYCHOANALYTIC TREATMENT IS MOST successful, analysands come to learn something surprising and disturbing about the process they have undergone. People enter analysis expecting that they will learn about their life history and about its impact on contemporary experience. This, they hope, will lead to a sense of control over themselves and to an evolving capacity to change in desired ways. But as analysis continues, we all come to realize—always slowly and painfully—that the idea of a consistently controlled and indelibly "adult" or "adapted" or "analyzed" sense of ourselves is mythic. Human experience is paradoxical and conflicted at its core, and even after the most successful analysis we are left with constant shifts in our sense of ourselves and of our circumstances. No matter how strong, confident, and fulfilled we are in one moment, there will always be a next moment in which we feel weak, frightened, and embattled. Analysis cannot immunize us against these shifts and the consequent uncertainties; it can only help us to live as fully and as creatively as possible amidst ambiguity and change.

Another unexpected (and often equally unpleasant) discovery that analysands make is that the past that they work to understand is neither as immutable nor as finally comprehensible as they hoped it would be. Instead of uncovering formed but forgotten memories, they discover that the exploration of the past leads mainly to recontextualization and reevaluation. Any event, they learn, can be seen in a virtually limitless number of ways, and any judgment about "what happened" depends on the perspective from which it is being viewed. Because our vantage point shifts constantly as life unfolds, history cannot be grasped and understood once and for all. Analysands learn that the idea of a fixed, static "past" is illusory; there is only what can be creatively elaborated at any moment. It is in this sense that psychoanalysis is most radically interminable.

To add to our confusion, this loss of curative influence does not seem to be caused by any diminution in the validity of our interpretive messages as such. Indeed, large segments of the analytic community have become convinced that therapeutic change is produced not through insight, but on the basis of a type of experience unprecedented in the analysand's past—a need-satisfying object relationship characterized by empathy (Kohut, 1977), (1984).

MODERN INTEREST IN COUNTERTRANSFERENCE as an inherent part of the psychoanalytic process is often cited as having begun with Heimann's (1950) classic paper "On Counter-Transference." Although there were several earlier papers on the subject that shared certain basic assumptions (Berman, 1948) ; (Winnicott, 1949), Heimann stated, perhaps most unequivocably (and most eloquently), that countertransference was not an aberration of standard technique, but a ubiquitous phenomena that had the potential, when recognized and worked with, for deepening the analyst's understanding of the patient. Heimann's emphasis was on the analyst's internal process of using countertransference as a resource for associating to and interpreting the patient's material.

Almost immediately after its publication, Little (1951) responded to Heimann's paper by stating that the analyst's awareness of countertransference experience was not enough. Little proposed that unless the analyst found a means of articulating his awareness of countertransference reactions to the patient, a reenactment of the patient's experience with parental figures would take place. In this event, the analyst would be colluding with the patient's resistance to keep certain perceptions and feelings about the analyst dissociated.

These positions represent fundamentally different approaches of utilizing countertransference. The premise of this article is that these two perspectives, which I call containing and responding, can be thought of as forming a dialectical relationship that can be used as a framework to process countertransference experience. This framework generates a creative tension when we consider the clinical choices to determine how we may best use countertransference to enhance the analytic exploration.

Containing is a familiar and well-established psychoanalytic concept. Heimann, Racker (1968), Winnicott (1949), (1951), (1958), and Bion (1970) have all made essential contributions to the concept.

Theodore Shapiro  

Introduction

IHAVE BEEN ASKED TO ADDRESS the reality of trauma. I think there is no doubt that there are events and occurrences in an individual's life that may be considered traumatic. However, just as the diagnosis of stress requires the concept of strain, there is no way to consider what is psychically traumatic only by observation from the outside. The word trauma, of course, is borrowed from physical medicine, in which the integrity of the body, the bones, the skin, is disrupted by an external impact. We are pretty sure, to a degree, that impacts beyond certain limits will invariably create traumatic effects on the body. In a similar vein, Freud (1893–1895) postulated that experiences in life, especially those of immature organisms or involving out-of-phase excitement, such as gross sexual arousal in children, could be overwhelming to the psyche. In fact, his earliest formulations include the idea that the essential feature of trauma entailed the condition that the psyche is flooded by stimuli, the consequences of which were disorganizing effects on cognition, irritability, psychological confusion, disruption of such physiologic cycles as sleep, etc.

Cooper (1986) recently described extreme trauma in a similar vein: "A psychological event which abruptly overwhelms the ego's capacity to provide a minimal sense of safety and integrative intactness" (p. 44). Many of these extreme disorganizations of patterned behavior are included in the current DSM III-IV definition of PTSD. On the other hand, memories of the eliciting events might be forgotten via the imposition of repression or in a vertical split by dissociation.

Those ideas were not strikingly different from what was already known in early postindustrial France and Austria. There had been an increase in reports and legal claims of psychic trauma as the consequence of accidents on the newly introduced railroads. Thus, the new transportation system may be said to have given rise to new disorders.

Ruth Imber Ph.D.

Ruth Imber

Ruth R. Imber, Ph.D.
390 West End Avenue
New York, NY 10024

Ruth Imber  

MASOCHISM IS UNDERSTOOD BY PSYCHOANALYSTS as the ability to derive pleasure from pain or as the pursuit of suffering (Glick & Meyers, 1988). While its psychoanalytic origins were imbedded in drive theory and the notion of a death instinct, the concept has been elaborated richly both from an ego-psychological and object-relations perspective. Perhaps because the concept was derived from classical Freudian theory, the interpersonal school of psychoanalysis has tended to disregard various phenomena that fall under the heading of masochistic behavior.

Although Sullivan dismissed the concept of masochism as "foggy thinking" (1953, p. 352), it seems to me he did recognize implicitly that it could be understood as an interpersonal tactic to influence others. He noted that real benefits could be derived through suffering, such as eliciting reassurance, sympathy, and even caretaking. But Sullivan did not apparently see any value in the idea that guilt may lead to self-punishment, which is a cornerstone of the classical theory of masochism. Today we know that masochistic behavior may serve relational needs, keeping one emotionally connected via identification to lost objects. It also may operate in conjunction with other character traits, such as narcissism (Cooper, 1988), to maintain a sense of personal identity, autonomy, and control.

I believe that there is a hint of this idea in Sullivan's notion of malevolent transformation. He observed that there were people who had learned, as children, the futility or even danger of seeking love or tenderness from their uncaring and rejecting caretakers. Rather than continue to suffer the hurt and disappointment of trying to get what was not available, such a child would instead learn to change his or her behavior from tenderness-seeking to angry rejection or mischievousness. While the need for tenderness went unmet, the malevolent transformation did protect against the pain and anxiety of being rejected or punished for seeking what was not to be had. And if the "malevolence" was met with punishment, that at least was under one's control.

IWOULD LIKE TO DISCUSS THE RESOLUTION of traumatic transference in analytic work with patients who have dissociative symptoms, and to suggest a technical modification of interpretation that allows for repair of the dissociated aspects of the self. I will argue that standard analytic technique based on a model of inner conflict as the basis for symptoms can actually be harmful and disruptive in work with these patients, if it imposes certain meanings prematurely. Interpersonal theory provides a more effective framework for understanding such dynamics, since it describes the development of the self through interaction with others, and may help to avoid the implication that abuse is the patient's fault.

By traumatic transference I mean a kind of transference in which the patient "unconsciously expects that the therapist, despite overt helpfulness and concern, will covertly exploit the patient for his or her own narcissistic gratification" (Spiegel, 1986, p. 72). That is, the transferential pattern is based on the patient's expectation of misuse of power by the parental or authoritative figure in the relationship. This dynamic leads to a replaying in all forms, in the analytic arena suspended in time and space, of some of the nastiest behaviors of the species. To be fully healed, and especially to be able to claim appropriate power for him or herself, the patient-victim-survivor may need to try out how it feels to be the abuser, as well as the victim (Davies & Frawley, 1992). In complement to the roles assumed by the patient, even the most well-intentioned analyst will be experienced as abusing his or her power at some point, and will certainly feel like, and possibly even be, the patient's victim at others. Herman (1992) describes how this happens.

The patient scrutinizes the therapist's every word and gesture, in an attempt to protect herself from the hostile reactions she expects.

In the manner that his colleagues have come to associate with him, Jay Greenberg has given us a thoughtful, sophisticated, and balanced discussion of an issue that is as important as it is controversial. One of those questions that not very long ago seemed a settled one—at least for many of us—the issue of self-disclosure on the part of the analyst has surfaced as an aspect of technique that deserves the kind of careful rethinking and reexamination with which Dr. Greenberg has approached it.

The need for review of a matter which, for most traditionally trained analysts, has essentially been a closed subject (self-disclosure being generally regarded as a breach of proper technique and, if persistent, an indication of unanalyzed character pathology) has come about parallel with, and is partially reflective of, changed and changing views of the analytic process.

For many members of this audience, this new perspective, one that views the analytic situation as inevitably involving the interplay of two psychologies; that acknowledges the substantial influence of covert or metacommunications on the analytic process; that regards objectivity and neutrality on the part of the analyst as relative rather than absolute matters; and that recognizes that the personality, predilections, and values of the analyst, along with certain of his countertransference responses, contribute in important ways both to his understanding of his patients and to the course and outcome of treatment, is anything but new. It is, in fact, one that is quite familiar, as many elements of it were articulated and made operational many years ago by analysts of the relational school. In this respect, our colleagues at the White Institute were way ahead of some of us Model T types and many of our so-called discoveries are less novel findings than awakenings; awakenings to aspects of the analytic process to which tradition, historical developments, and political considerations have blinded us.

Psychic Deadness: Freud

Michael Eigen Ph.D.

Michael Eigen

Michael Eigen, Ph.D.
225 Central Park West, #10A
New York, NY 10024

Michael Eigen  

THE SENSE OF BEING DEAD has become a popular clinical theme. More people than in the past seek help for feeling dead. Although feeling dead is a central complaint of many individuals, it is not clear where this deadness comes from, or what can be done about it.

There are many variations of psychic deadness. For some people, deadness does not consume much psychic space. It is a circumscribed counterpole or subtheme in a fuller, richer existence. It comes and goes or nags in the background. At times it becomes prepossessing, and one wonders (with a chill) what one would do if it swallowed existence, if it became all there was. One waits for it to fade and usually it does. It moves along with a variety of moods and states of being.

Some people have pockets of deadness that are relatively constant. They get used to living with areas of deadness. They wish they were more alive, that life offered more, but they make do with their portion. If life is decent enough, a bit of deadness is not too much to pay for satisfactions. One adapts to being less than one might be, to feeling less than one might feel. One talks oneself into imagining one is about as happy as one can be, as happy as one is going to be. One more or less succeeds in believing oneself, since one fears (rightly) that things could be worse.

For some people, the sense of deadness is pervasive. They describe themselves as zombies, the walking dead, empty and unable to feel. An extreme example of massive deadness was an anorexic-bulimic woman, Deborah, who passed through my office several years ago. She weighed under eighty pounds and looked like a corpse. Her bones were like piercing icicles that stung and ripped me apart.

I wept upon hearing her story, a familiar story, yet shocking in its outcome. Deborah's parents were successful professionals. There was a history of neglect, a mixture of over- and understimulation, the usual story of emotional poverty in a luxurious setting. Overeating-vomiting-starving parodied the too much-too little that characterized her life.

RESISTANCE" IS NOT A WORD I ORDINARILY USE, either conceptually or clinically, and when I might hear it inadvertently pop out of my mouth it is usually when I am feeling grouchy with a patient and unaware that I wish to conceal it. Notwithstanding its illusory advantage in a countertransferential emergency, it is a term that I feel has become largely incompatible with the natural evolution in postclassical analytic thought. In effect, it traps us into preserving intact Freud's (1925) formulation of the function of negation, in which the negativity of resistance is viewed as a barrier between depth and surface designed to prevent repressed images or ideas from entering consciousness. In this sense, it is a remnant of our past that I think can be usefully reframed as part-of an enacted dialectical process of meaning construction, rather than an archeological barrier preventing the surfacing of disavowed reality.

Freud (1925, p. 235–236) observed that "the content of a repressed image or idea can make its way into consciousness, on condition that it is negated. Stephen Mitchell  

ANYONE WHO HAS TRIED to keep up with the psychoanalytic literature of recent years has learned, probably with a good deal of exasperation, that psychoanalytic theorizing has become enormously complex and variegated, with many different authors writing from different theoretical traditions, with different terms, about many different facets of clinical process, the nature of mind, and psychic development. It is very difficult to study or master even a small area or single line of this great complexity. Yet, if one steps back from the particularities, the variations, and the details, certain broad themes and common concerns emerge.

One of those themes has been the movement, over the past 40 years in the history of psychoanalytic ideas, from a view of mind as monadic, a separable, individual entity, to a view of mind as dyadic, emerging from and inevitably embedded within a relational field. This shift has had a major, dramatic impact on theorizing about the analytic situation, classically conceived as a neutral medium within which the mind of one person, the patient, emerged, unravelled, and gradually displayed itself. It is difficult to find this traditional model employed in its original, pristine form by any contemporary school of analytic thought, including the most classical Freudian. Even the most conservative authors now regard the analyst as having some impact on the analytic process. The blank screen, like the 8-millimeter movie projector, seems on its way to becoming an antique, and analytic neutrality and anonymity are regularly described as, at best, ideals, and at worst, illusions. The analytic process is often now generally understood to represent not simply an unfolding of the contents of the patient's mind, but an interaction between two people, each of whom brings with them their own dynamics, passions, ideas, and general subjectivity.

SUMMARY

The narrative of self is conceived in terms of the stream of consciousness. Consequently, it cannot be defined by its contents, since the metaphorical stream is in constant flux, endlessly changing and never repeated. Rather, self depends upon a particular form of mental activity, which resembles play (Meares & Lichtenberg, 1995), and which is associational and nonlinear. Where this activity is manifest in words, it can be called a "narrative of self." This "narrative" is frequently interrupted, in the clinical situation, by another system of mental activity that has a different form. It is fixed, rather than dynamic and progressive, and is associated with negative affect. It represents a repetition in the present of a past anxiety, in which the effect of the caregiving environment had been damaging to a developing sense of self. This malignant system, described by Brandchaft, functions as if automatically. The individual may be relatively unaware of its operation. It is triggered internally by states of well-being that are characteristic of a sense of self.

In this article, Brandchaft's description is amplified in terms of Tulving's distinction between episodic and semantic memory. It is postulated that episodic memory, which develops at about the age of four, is the basis of the stream of consciousness, and so, of self. It involves reflective awareness. The fixed system of negating evaluations is seen to reside in a module of memory that develops earlier than episodic memory. This form of memory, semantic, concerns knowledge of facts. The system is relatively sequestered from the stream of consciousness, and the origins of its "facts" are no longer accessible. The therapeutic aim is to integrate this system into the more mature form of consciousness underpinned by episodic memory.

Introduction

FOR SOME TIME I HAVE believed that nonverbal communication is as important for the evolution of the psychoanalytic process as the patient's verbalized free associations. Because we have focused most of our attention on the spoken language of our analysands in order to work out its latent meaning, we may have neglected to observe nonverbal language more closely, thus preventing us from discovering the rich source of unconscious fantasies contained in their silence, gestures, movements, and facial expressions.

It has been said that silence can embrace an enormous spectrum of different meanings: resentment, rage, shyness, panic, sadness, anxiety, emptiness, boredom, indifference, frustration, arrogance, etc. However, in general it has been considered as a resistance, impeding the psychoanalytic process. The so-called silent patients very often cause irritation in many analysts, who then actively try to make them speak at all costs, so that the analysis might be—according to them—truly productive. However, silence is not always obstructing, cold, hostile, and ominous; it can also be warm, kind, fruitful, and elaborative. Silence, along with gestures and movements, are all specific modes of object relations through which patients try to transmit messages that they are unable to formulate in the spoken language. Racker (1952) pointed out that music is a succession of sounds and silences. Bion (1974) spoke of "fruitful silences" and silences that are worthless "mathematically"; in other words, they are equivalent to "zero." But there are occasions when that "zero" is placed between two "1s, " and it then becomes 101. Similarly, certain silences convert the sounds preceding and following them into valuable communications. For Greenson (1961), there exists between silence and the spoken word a range of sounds, cries, whispers, laughs, groans, etc., full of emotional content.

SUMMARY

Play and language are intermingled in human development. The language that accompanies play is a manifestation of a mental activity that is nonlinear and associative. Early play, which depends on reciprocity and a sequencing of behaviors, may foster the evolution of the sequencing of behavior and language that is characteristic of symbolic play, which first shows itself after about 18 months. The stories the child tells in this setting are personal, and concerned with the representation of a personal reality. At this stage of life, we see the beginning of "the linguistic construction of self in time" (Nelson, 1989). The emergence of the narrative of self depends on caregivers, who provide "attunement, " "resonance, " and a sense of "fit." Out of the sense of fit evolves not only a patterned associative style of language but a feeling of well-being.

61

Where this enabling atmosphere is deficient, or where there is direct impingement, for example, through abuse, the child has relatively little access to the associative activity that subserves the subjective and "inner" aspects of personal existence. The development of self is impeded and the individual's mental processes are dominated by a linear, externally directed form of thought. He or she lives as if addicted to the stimuli of the outer world. In addition, no sense of well-being can be gained. Furthermore, the associative sequencing, which binds together otherwise disconnected elements of psychic life, is lost. The result is "fragmentation" and a loss of personal continuity.

SUMMARY

The germs of the concept of the curative fantasy are present in Kohut's writings and—as I indicated earlier—he considered this to be an aspect of a selfobject transference:

Patients who often present severe defects in their self-esteem and self-cohesion are analyzable because their developmental needs, while insufficiently responded to in childhood, had yet retained the capacity for reasserting their claim. … The self psychologist's understanding of the legitimacy of the needs of the self leads, via subtle change in the mode of his communications, perhaps in particular via a changed tone of voice, to an atmosphere which is especially in tune with the requirements with the narcissistically damaged patient, as he remobilizes the old childhood needs of a self that strives to achieve vitality, harmony and coherence" (Kohut, 1979, p. 479).

The clinical example demonstrated that it may not be in the clinical setting and not necessarily in relation to the analyst that unmet developmental needs become remobilized, but rather, that such remobilization may occur in marriages and other intimate relationships. Expectedly, in these relationships such infantile wishes become repeatedly frustrated and patients become more, rather then less, symptomatic. If, in a therapeutic situation, these transference expectations are recognized and the

122

symptomatic behavior systematically interpreted, a genuine healing process is set into motion. It is then that patients become available to accept needed selfobject responses even when these do not conform to their more infantile expectations. In the case of Dr. White, his ability to use his son's unconditional love, experiencing himself as a significant person in his son's life, became a crucial element in the transformation of his curative fantasy, and with that, in his ultimate recovery.

The discussion of the clinical material had demonstrated the heuristic value of recognizing and actively interpreting the curative fantasy that, because of its unacceptability, had become a constituent of the symptomatic behavior: only being sick and miserable could give "legitimacy" to what the patient experienced as "childish wishes."

This has begun to bring fresh perspectives to the field. Depression is often listed as one of the prominent symptoms in posttraumatic clinical syndromes. I want to consider here the effect depression has on the crucial process of remembering and of recovery in traumatic states, and some of the ways it contributes negatively to an already difficult mourning process. Gilead Nachmani, Ph.D.

Gilead Nachmani  

WE SEE THE SYMPTOMATIC EFFECTS OF TRAUMA in an intriguing form of memory: not knowing. Not knowing is often the first response to trauma. It reflects the moment of breakdown, the sudden confusion of impact, of being overwhelmed by the stunning shock where everything adaptive fails, except for the obliteration of knowledge

As Laub and Auerhahn (1993) observe, it is the nature of trauma to elude knowledge. Perhaps it is also the self-protective function of knowledge to elude trauma. Ignorance in the presence of anguish is often the signature of trauma. To survive it, the knowledge of trauma needs to be deflected, hidden, disconnected from ordinary experiential knowledge Thinking about something that is so overwhelming that it cannot be thought about is something of an impossibility.

Trauma is overwhelming. Virtually nothing that is known by the victim can prepare for it, and nothing that the victim does can avoid it. It must be endured against the wishes of the victim, without self-protection or the protection of another person upon whom the victim has depended. Among the most powerful effects of trauma, is the intrusive disruption of conscious and unconscious thinking. As a result, trauma cannot be symbolically represented. When conscious and unconscious processes are disrupted, the skills that they have come to build—meaning, cognitive structure, sign recognition, symbol formation, syntax, differentiation, discrimination, and the availability to use these capacities to formulate and organize language—are either absent or are present but ineffectual. It appears that the need to save or preserve the self involves the abrupt disconnection of self from its capacities to perceive, think, and feel coherently. Descriptively, this is dissociation.

Helplessness is among the common elements of trauma. It is a failure in self-protection. Because of the stunning disruption of thinking, as well as the helplessness, the subsequent perception of trauma by the victim is less than representational.

I AM DELIGHTED TO HAVE THIS OPPORTUNITY to review Arthur Feiner's contributions to the psychoanalytic literature, both in his role as Editor in Chief of Contemporary Psychoanalysis and as a prolific author in his own right. We have a long history of collaboration that goes back to the early 1950s College Drop-out Project at the William Alanson White Psychoanalytic Institute, and we have, over the years, shared many ideas and coauthored a few papers. Since a great many of my articles have been published in Contemporary Psychoanalysis under his stewardship, and since Arthur personally, and at considerable sacrifice of his time and effort, edited and published my last book, it is evident that I am hardly unbiased in both my gratitude to him and my admiration of his thinking (and good taste in authors!).

In an introduction to one of my articles, Arthur once referred to me as "the Fred Astaire of psychoanalysis" (Feiner, 1978, p. 31). In reviewing his articles, it occurred to me that he might well be considered a combination of Isaiah Berlin and Zorba the Greek! As as a polymath (the kind of abstruse word he loves), he combines a very wide-ranging intellectual curiosity and erudition, complemented by an antic exuberance, an in-your-eye candor and outspokenness, which is manifest in his article in the November 1992 issue of this journal.

Initially, I was not too taken with being compared with Fred Astaire, since it might have implied mere fancy footwork—superficiality—rather than a (presumably) light, sophisticated touch. Besides, I am the only person I know who doesn't think Astaire is a national treasure. But I am now convinced that it was meant as a genuine compliment, since Art much admires Astaire's terpsichore; Balanchine himself once said that Astaire was one of two major influences on his work. I don't know how Arthur will take all this. I'm sure that he admires Berlin's questing mind—I'm not so sure how he regards Zorba. Nevertheless, Zorba and Berlin mirror the conjuncture of the Apollonian and Dionysian mentalities so often referred to in his writings and so manifest in his style and personality.

IT IS DIFFICULT TO OVERESTIMATE Melanie Klein's impact on psychoanalytic thinking. So many of her locutions and concerns are part of psychoanalytic daily life. She shares with nineteenth century psychiatry, poetry, and gothic literature an obsession with splitting. In Klein's writings, splits in personality become splits in ego, object, and affect. She embarks on what may well be one of the most detailed portrayals of psychological splitting in the history of ideas. She shares this preoccupation with Freud and Jung, but gives it her own turn, takes it to places the founders of depth psychology did not quite get to. If the idea of splitting is popular today, Melanie Klein is a background influence.

Klein shares with existentialism a preoccupation with death. Our sense of self, other, and time is stained by death on the horizon. For Freud and Klein, death is not only a definitive event approaching us, but something working in every psychic pore now. Klein spins variants of Freud's death drive throughout her work. She takes seriously Freud's insistence that Eros and the death instinct permeate every fiber of psychic life. How death work and life work contribute to every psychic event involves "problems whose elucidation would be the most rewarding achievement of psychological research" (Freud, 1937, p. 243). Klein immerses herself in death and life processes to contribute toward the elucidation Freud invites.

Klein makes psychoanalysis more honest by making explicit its implicit concern with psychosis. In an earlier contribution (Eigen, 1986, pp. 5–31), I showed how an underlying concern with madness contributed to Freud's structural concepts and descriptions of psychic processes. He applied notions drawn from psychotic phenomenology to treatment of neurotics. Klein tears the veil away and focuses on psychotic anxieties, mechanisms, and defenses that make their way through infancy and remain active all life long. She gives credence to the intuition that madness runs through human affairs and plays a role in everyday life.

IN MY EXPERIENCE, program committees tend to assemble groups of discussants who represent different viewpoints, expecting that the debate among them will prove educational for the audience. I believe that I was invited as a spokesman for the traditional, or classical position, at least in part because I have written one paper pertaining to the topic of the analyst's self-revelation as a technical issue, which I will discuss later. I hope that neither you, the audience, nor the inviting committee will be too disappointed to discover that, far from engaging Dr. Greenberg in debate, I shall try to sing in harmony with his thematic exposition.

There is no doubt in my mind that Freud's cautionary notes about the risks of self-revelation are, as Dr. Greenberg asserts, the advice "of a clinician who has tried something many times and who has lived to regret the consequences." They were set forth in papers intended for the instruction of the inexperienced practitioner, in the early morning, if not quite the dawn, of psychoanalytic history. I would add, as I do to students at my Institute, that Freud's well-known suggestion that the analyst be like a mirror to his patients was intended in the same spirit. It was his way of saying that it does not good for the analyst to try to help his patients change their neurotic difficulties by using himself as an example, that is, by describing his own troubles and his methods of overcoming them. Forget that time-honored device of the well-intended, Freud suggested, and concentrate instead solely on what the patient has to reveal of the nature of his problems (and he might have added, believe me, I have tried the other and it does not work).

I am totally in agreement with Dr. Greenberg's astute distinction between deliberate, consciously intended self-disclosure, and the inevitable self-revelations that are the consequence of our presentation of ourselves and our technical choices, which range from our choice of waiting room furniture to our selection of interventions.

SUMMARY

Projective identification is definitionally indistinguishable from projection because it always operates in an object-relations context; i.e., the projecting subject needs an object to warrant the illusion that the latter can contain the projection. It is a primitive as well as sophisticated mechanism that runs the gamut from defensive, evacuative disavowal, through regressively hibernative dedifferentiation from (fusion with) the object, through vicarious participation with objects and manipulative control of them, to, ultimately, sublimated empathic resonance with them. It is the agent of preverbal communication between the infant and its mother and is also a form of signalling and posturing. It is the source of all anxiety (as opposed to normal fear and concern) and of all persecution (as opposed to realistic danger). It is the architectural instrument par excellence for the creation of the internal objects that comprise the structures of the internal world, for the distortion of, or transference to, the objects of the external world, and is largely responsible for the creation of superegos. It is most manifest when we take life events "personally, " that is, subjectively. It saturates the manifest and latent content of all psychoanalyses in its role as projected "alter egos, " which are signifiers of the self at one remove.

Projective identification is a principal participant in the transference/countertransference situation. As the patient projects his own disidentifications into the image of the analyst (actually, into the potential space existing between them), the recipient analyst seeks to contain these projective

501

identifications by introjective trial identification with them, toward which the analyst may have a counter-reaction in the form of a projective counteridentification and/or countertransference proper. All three forms of these "countertransferences" can be subclassified into "forced" and "unforced." These varieties of responses, in addition to the analyst's other therapeutic instruments, such as intuition, introspection, sensation, and perception (observation), constitute what I propose to call "the countertransference complex."

In the course of any analysis, but especially in cases of trauma, abuse, and primitive mental disorders, there is not only a tendency for the patient to develop a transference neurosis/psychosis from his or her infantile neurosis/psychosis, but there is also a tendency for the analyst to develop a countertransference neurosis/psychosis commensurate with and complementary to that of the patient. The combination of the transference and countertransference neuroses/psychoses is exemplified bilaterally in the images of the Crucifixion and the Pietà and in the phenomenon of exorcism.

He has given us a glimpse into his own thought process regarding disclosure of this particular kind and I think we are all appreciative of this, even if we would not necessarily work the same way.

FROM THE MOMENT of its invention, the psychoanalytic method thrilled Freud and his followers. In one stroke, it seemed, Freud had given us a technique that promised radical therapeutic results for previously untreatable illnesses, and that also offered a scientific approach to exploring the human soul. As time went on, however, questions arose about the power of the method to cure. When indications for analysis were broadened so that not only the symptom neuroses but also the character disorders were treated, the very concept of cure became increasingly vague. Eventually, even claims that symptoms could be permanently abolished seemed infused by wishful thinking. Freud himself became a therapeutic pessimist.

Despite these developments, everybody could see that something happens in the consulting room that grips the human imagination. In the course of analyzing his patients, Freud evolved a vision of human nature so compelling that it shaped the intellectual life of an entire century. Admiring science and disdaining philosophy, Freud insisted that we had his method to thank for what we had learned; anybody who followed the correct procedure would arrive at the same discoveries he did. So psychoanalysts are left with a paradox: Our method outshines our results, which can be ephemeral, even ineffable. The effects of analysis are notoriously difficult to quantify, to demonstrate convincingly, or to compare with the reports of therapists using more pedestrian techniques. Our special claim lies less in what we do than in how we do it. We have idealized our method.

Conclusion and Summary

The unconscious from a two-person psychology perspective consists of internalized interpersonal configurations that have been unarticulated and that continue to exert control over the course of one's life. These configurations serve as templates that guide one's expectancies and interpretations of events but interfere with the ability to form new self-experiences and to develop new ways of being. This interpersonal unconscious becomes "known" as it is experienced by both the patient and the analyst in the here-and-now of the transference-countertransference matrix. Both participants are unable to step outside of their own subjectivity. Discovering the absolute unconscious is less important than the articulation of repetitive and internalized patterns of relating and the ultimate expansion of experience. This does not mean that the concept of unconscious is insignificant. On the contrary, unformulated and unarticulated interpersonal configurations are seen as the substance of unconscious. What has changed is what is done with this unconscious experience. The archeological pursuit of absolute truth and the illusion that the analyst

274

can be a nonparticipating, objective interpreter, or an objective facilitator, dictates a positivistic analytic stance. The interpersonally informed analyst lives out unconscious experience—the unformulated and unarticulated internalized relational configurations—as they are mutually enacted in the therapeutic field. It is through the repetition and articulation of these engagements that patients work their way out of safe but limiting patterns of experience. The analyst who acknowledges unwitting interaction must repeat the old and destructive internalized configurations before anything genuinely new can develop. Awareness of participation occurs postenactment.

MY PATIENT CAN INTRODUCE HIMSELF with the first dream he reported in treatment.

I dreamt I was a secret agent. I had some sort of secret information so important that I'd been obliged to take cyanide to keep it from being found out. Only I woke up the next day—it hadn't been enough to kill me. Then this distant friend came to take me to a safe house, which involved leading me through a sort of college campus. We came across the enemy Russian agent, who was playing tennis. I think he wanted me to play against him. I remember taunting him, getting him good and angry. Then at the safe house I remember saying good-bye to my wife and son, matter-of-factly, and taking enough more cyanide to kill me.

We meet here a man poisoned with self-containment. He had sought out psychotherapy at his wife's insistence. His irritability, emotional distancing, and lifelong depression were strangling their marriage. The dream occurred after two months of treatment, during which he had sketched out the picture of a bleak and lonely childhood, marred by humiliation, rejection, and betrayal. An association to the dream was that the Russian agent looked like me. CONTEMPORARY PSYCHOANALYSIS HAS BEEN CHARACTERIZED by a growing appreciation of the impact of the analyst's subjectivity on the analytic process. The analyst is understood as a "constructionist" (Hoffman, 1991), (1992) who creates as well as discovers the meaning of what transpires in the course of the analysis. According to Mitchell (1993), human experience is fundamentally ambiguous, so that to understand something means to organize it in a particular manner. Experience is always open to multiple interpretations, interpretations that may be opposite, conflicting, and seemingly irreconcilable. As a reflection of her own subjectivity, the analyst employs her own "organizing principles" to create order out of ambiguity. According to Atwood and Stolorow (1984), the need to maintain the organization of experience is a supraordinate motivational principle. And it might be noted that analysts do not necessarily possess any single set of clear and coherent organizing principles. They possess multiple organizing principles, some conflicting and some unconscious, despite the striving to establish a unitary sense of order without internal contradiction.

In studying the analyst's contribution to the psychoanalytic situation, two primary sources of the analyst's subjectivity have been articulated: the analyst's unique personality and the analyst's theoretical orientation. When the analyst's individual personality is examined, the analyst's subjective contribution is considered to be the analyst's countertransference. Beginning with the seminal work of Racker (1968), there has been an assumption that the analyst's countertransference is a reflection of the interpersonal situation that patient and analyst have cocreated out of the unique interaction of their individual personalities. The analyst's most private and most personal experience in the analytic situation reflects some aspect of the transference/countertransference dynamic in the analytic relationship.

Violence and abuse within marital and dating relationships has been an area of growing concern and attention among therapists and social researchers alike over the last two decades. During this period, a range of societal, circumstantial, and personality factors have been implicated as predictors of dyadic violence (e.g., patriarchal norms, socioeconomic hardships, alcohol use, low self-esteem). However, research thus far has largely failed to conclusively isolate any one factor as associated with the use of dyadic violence. Instead, violent and abusive treatment of a partner appears to depend upon a constellation of cultural, situational, and personality factors that shape the perception a person has of both self and others. Unfortunately, as this area of investigation has evolved, there has been a relative absence of comprehensive theoretical frameworks that might provide greater clarity and inferential understanding to the possible dynamics underlying these factors. Recent psychoanalytic contributions concerning narcissistic character pathology and dimensions of shame may provide one such theoretical framework for understanding a partner's readiness to use or sustain abuse within a relationship. In this article, two recently proposed styles of narcissistic disturbance will be discussed as possibly underlying many of those characteristics observed within violent relationships. The issue of shame, which has been recently linked to both interpersonal violence (Scheff & Retzinger, 1991) and narcissistic pathology (Wright, O'Leary, & Balkin, 1989), has particular application. Additionally, the way in which shame is handled and expressed may be significantly influenced by gender; men and women may develop diverging styles of narcissism. Partners representing these two diverging styles may enter into abusive relationships in response to projective identification of complementary needs.

THE CONCEPT OF "EXPRESSED EMOTION" (EE) represents one of the most important discoveries in the field of psychosocial treatment of schizophrenia over the last decades. According to a recent review (Kavanagh, 1992, p. 616), it "may prove to be the most significant treatment breakthrough in schizophrenia since the discovery of neuroleptic medication." The discharge of many patients from psychiatric hospitals and their management in the community brought new problems to the attention of mental health professionals and patients' families. The importance of EE studies derives from the possibility, offered by these studies, to test, through a rigorous methodology, a psychosocial approach to the treatment of schizophrenia.

THE CELEBRATION OF THE FIFTIETH anniversary of the White Institute, 1993, with a clinical conference and two days of reminiscences of founders, involved an in-depth view of innovations within the interpersonal psychoanalytic heritage. Given this framework, I chose to focus my clinical views and my work on a difficult type of patient, to whom I give the old label, masochistic personality. I would like to discuss my understanding of masochism, and my work with such a patient over many years of treatment. This patient suffered sexual abuse in his childhood; our work with that early trauma is part of the presentation.

Interpersonal Psychoanalysis

Let me first make a few general observations about interpersonal psychoanalysis. It is open-ended and pluralistic. The psychoanalytic work centers on meanings and motivations as the patient tells his story. The patient as narrator (Spence, 1982) describes moments of experience in detail, and the analyst helps organize and reveal meanings in the narrated experience, other than those the patient is encapsulated in. The "analytic work" thereby reframes the patient's understanding of his reality by deconstructing the meanings he gives to his experience. A quote from Wallace Stevens's (1954) "The Man with the Blue Guitar" comes to mind.

The man bent over his guitar,

A shearsman of sorts. The day was green.

They said, "You have a blue guitar,

You do not play things as they are."

The man replied, "Things as they are

Are changed upon the blue guitar."

SUMMARY

The relationship of the two brothers was intense, mutually entangled and dependent, ambivalent, and symbiotic. They were tied to each other by the closest bonds, and when that connection was ever threatened by circumstance, conflict, separation, or hostility, both suffered pangs of separation and abandonment. They could not live without each other, and as the events proved, they could not live with each other. But their fates were intertwined from the beginning. They were in a sense psychic twins, mutual mirrors each to the other, doubles in a profound psychic sense. For Vincent, it was his connection with Theo that preserved his life and made his artistic creativity possible. For Theo, it was his connection with his eccentric, erratic, troubled, and dependent brother that gave meaning and sustenance to his life as well. They could share an artistic vision and a fantasy of mutual involvement in the creative process that consumed them both.
